newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Japan says Malaysia, Philippines, NZ to join ITA.
newsitem.headline: Japan says Malaysia, Philippines, NZ to join ITA.

text.p: Malaysia, the Philippines and New Zealand are likely to join an agreement to scrap tariffs on information technology products by the year 2000, Japanese officials said on Friday.
"Malaysia wants to join but needs some more time to consider," a Japanese trade official told reporters.

Malaysia issued a statement earlier on Friday saying it was unable yet to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO) information technology agreement but welcomed the objective to eliminate duties on high-tech products.

"Malaysia is not able to join this initiative at this juncture, due to the need to undertake a thorough analysis of product coverage and to have the necessary internal consultations with the affected parties to decide on the products in which offers could be made," Malaysia's minister of International Trade and Industry Rafidah Aziz said.
Government approval would be secured for Malaysia's participation in the initiative after completion of the analysis and consultations, she said.
The Japanese officials said Manila had also expressed its desire to join the agreement, unveiled on the closing day of the inaugural WTO ministerial meeting.
"Both the Philippines and Malaysia will join the negotiations in January," the official said.

Ministers from 29 countries said in a draft declaration that they would scrap tariffs on infotech products beginning in 1997 and ending in 2000 "recognising that extending staging of reductions and, before implementation, expansion of product coverage may be necessary in limited circumstances."
The Japanese officials also said they expected New Zealand to join the accord, further details of which are to be worked out at negotiations in Geneva in January.
New Zealand's current domestic political situation had made it difficult for Wellington to make a decision to join now, they said.

The Japanese officials said the addition of those three countries would likely mean that ITA participants would account for the about 90 percent of world trade in infotech products needed to implement the tariff elimination pact.
Already, countries that have agreed to the Information Technology Agreement account for "well over" 80 percent of world trade in these products, the draft ministerial declaration said.
Japanese Trade Minister Shinji Sato welcomed the IT agreement, which covers some 300 items including microchips, computers, computer software and telecom-related products.

"Further growth can be expected in the information technology sector in the future. The elimination of tariffs will bring major benefits not only to Japan but to many countries," Sato said in a statement issued in Tokyo.
Sato was unable to attend the WTO conference because of a domestic scandal linking ministry bureaucrats to an oil wholesaler arrested for tax evasion.
